title: Review: today's work — MIME/S/MIME crate overhaul
notes:
Maintainer risk: LOW — the codebase is well-structured, trait-based keys are correctly abstracted, Zeroizing is applied correctly, and non_exhaustive is consistently used. The main risks are the CEK error message chain-index attribution (MIME-e7k.1) and the signed-content CRLF boundary ambiguity (MIME-e7k.2).
Confidence: 75% chance of missed bug. Least confident flags: (1) MIME-e7k.2 (signed CRLF) — the round-trip test passes, which either means the issue doesn't exist or the test's byte extraction coincidentally excludes the CRLF. Need to read what mail-parser records as body_range for the first part of a multipart/signed vs what sign() actually hashed. (2) MIME-e7k.1 (pkix-chain index ordering) — requires reading pkix-chain source to confirm whether indices are leaf-first or root-first. Uncertainty driven by: not reading pkix-chain source code. Would raise confidence if: ran a test with a deliberately bad intermediate cert and checked whether the error message names the right cert.
Idiom rating: ACCEPTABLE — The codebase uses idiomatic Rust patterns throughout: non_exhaustive, ? operator, proper error types, no unsafe, no Box<dyn Error> in API. The main non-idiomatic spots are (1) SmimeError::Other used for signature errors in verify_sig (MIME-e7k.16), (2) silent DER encode failure in cycle detection (MIME-e7k.18), and (3) missing Display on three public algorithm enums (MIME-e7k.17). The expect() panics in encrypt_aes_cbc closures are justified by invariants but non-local. No Rc/Arc, no gratuitous clones, no index loops where iterators fit better.
Rust idiom confidence: 80% chance of missed issue. Least confident flags: the closures in encrypt_aes_cbc with expect() — I believe they cannot panic given the structure, but a reader has to trace the invariant across function boundaries. Uncertainty driven by: not having traced every code path exhaustively. Would raise confidence if: clippy --all-features passes clean (already tested above — it does).
